Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Eleven are still usable, but several need parts soon, and the other seven are too worn for us to lend out. We're not asking you to choose for us or place an order; a clear estimate and a few practical choices would be useful for our next volunteer meeting on May 14.

The group has riders from about eight to sixteen years old, with a lot of first-timers and some who are comfortable riding but are still learning turns and stopping. We use the same boards on smooth concrete inside the covered court and on the rougher path around its edge. We don't need boards for ramps or high-speed riding. Our coaches say stability and easy-to-understand setups matter more than having the latest parts. One parent described the existing loaners as “a mixed bag from three different decades,” which is fair, although two of them have been repaired carefully and still work well.

Could you suggest a sensible mix of complete boards and replacement parts? We have been thinking of twelve standard street-style boards and six shorter cruisers, but that's only a starting point, not a fixed requirement. For the street boards, the riders who use them most often are usually comfortable with decks around 8.0 to 8.25 inches wide. We'd like to know whether a slightly wider option would be easier for beginners to balance on, without making the boards awkward for smaller riders. For the cruisers, we were picturing something around 28 to 30 inches long, but we haven't tried a lot of different shapes. Please tell us if those dimensions are a poor match for how we'll use them.

1. For the boards and parts, please show an economical option and a more durable option, with the price for each complete setup and a short note about what changes between them. We don't have a preferred brand. We would rather have standard parts that can be replaced later than unusual pieces that are difficult to find. The wheels on several current boards have flattened spots, and one rider said, “these wheels feel like shopping carts on the rough path.” We don't know if that means a softer wheel would help or if those wheels are simply worn out. Could you explain what you recommend for the two surfaces, including wheel size and hardness, and flag any trade-offs?

2. We can reuse some of the current hardware if it passes inspection, so please don't count all 18 boards as needing a full replacement. The trucks on four boards seem straight and move freely, but we haven't measured them or checked every mounting hole. Two decks have chipped edges without obvious cracks, and one has a crack near a truck mounting hole; we have taken that board out of use. Please let us know which parts you would want us to bring in before you could say whether they're safe to reuse. If it's easier, a separate estimate for replacing the worn wheels, bearings, grip tape, and basic mounting hardware would help us compare repair against buying complete setups. We don't want to repair the cracked deck.

We also need protective equipment for the loaner shelf. At the moment we have nine helmets in mixed sizes, and we don't know whether all of them still meet current requirements. Please price six additional helmets, if you can, in a range that covers smaller and larger youth heads, and tell us what sizing information you need from us. We'd also like eight sets of knee and elbow pads, plus wrist guards for riders who want them. We don't need you to assume one size will fit everyone. If you offer a sizing chart or a way to try samples, please include that in your response. Our volunteers can help riders adjust equipment, but they are not trained to certify used helmets.

Storage is another concern because the shed gets damp in winter, though water has not pooled on the floor. We can put equipment on a shelf about 48 inches wide and 20 inches deep. A wall rack might be possible, but we would have to ask the library before attaching anything, so please treat that as uncertain rather than part of the request. The helmets currently get stacked in a plastic bin, which makes it hard to see the sizes. Could you suggest a basic way to store the boards and protective gear without assuming we can install permanent fixtures? Please list any storage item separately from the riding equipment so we can leave it out if needed.

Our target is to stay near $2,400 including tax and delivery, but it is not a hard cap and we don't want safety items removed just to reach it. If the useful options go above that amount, please show the total and identify what could be purchased later without making the initial loaner set unsuitable. We can collect a local order if that changes the delivery cost, but we can't pick it up before May 10. If an item is not available by then, please mark that clearly and give an estimated restock date only if you have one; an estimate is fine, and we understand it may change.

Could you send the prices with tax and delivery shown separately, and note whether assembly is included or needs to be done by our volunteers? It would also help to have product links or model names, warranty information if available, and your usual time frame for replacing a part that breaks. We can send photos of the boards and the shelf, but we'd rather not guess at truck measurements or helmet sizes. If you need those details to make a recommendation, please tell us exactly what to measure or photograph. We can bring the questionable boards by the shop after 4 p.m. on a weekday, if that would make the reuse estimate more reliable. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i went to the northside electronics club on tuesday evening, mostly because mara said they were looking at an old shortwave receiver that had belonged to her uncle. i had not been to the club before. it meets in the back room of a community workshop on ash street, and the entrance is through a side door beside the bicycle racks. i arrived a little after six, while rain was still coming off the awning. the room smelled like wet coats, warm dust, and the coffee someone had left on a hot plate. there were six people there when i came in, maybe seven if the person in the doorway was already part of the group.

mara was setting the receiver on a green cutting mat, and she told me, “it was working when he put it away, but that could have been ten years ago.” the case was brown, with a carrying handle that had a crack near one screw. a paper label inside the lid said “R. Vale, 1978,” though nobody knew if that was the owner or the year. mara said it had been kept in a cupboard in her uncle’s shed, and she was not sure whether it had ever got damp. she had brought the power cord separately, wrapped in a grocery bag, because the insulation looked stiff. no one plugged it in right away.

tom, who seemed to run the bench for the evening, asked everyone to say what they had brought and what they hoped to do. he had a small transistor radio with a loose tuning knob, and he said he was only borrowing the club’s soldering iron. luis brought a cardboard box of resistors sorted into envelopes, although some of the handwriting was fading. i had brought a cheap digital multimeter and a notebook, but i had no project. mara laughed and said, “then you can be the person who remembers which screw came from where.” she had laid out three shallow trays beside the receiver, and tom put the screws from the back panel into the first one.

we started by looking at the outside and the controls, without applying power. the dial moved smoothly, but the pointer stopped just short of the lower end of its scale. one corner of the front grille was pushed inward, and there was a faint rattle when tom tilted the case. he took off the back panel with a short screwdriver and set it on a folded towel. inside, the wiring looked tidy to me, but there was a gray film on the metal shield and some dust caught around the speaker. luis pointed to a small stain near the transformer and said it might just be old adhesive. he did not sound certain. tom asked us not to brush anything away yet, because he wanted a picture before cleaning.

1. things we checked before power
- the power cord jacket had a split near the plug, so mara kept it in the bag.
- the fuse holder was present, but the label beside it was too worn to read clearly.
- the speaker cone had no obvious tear, though the paper edge looked dry.
- the battery compartment had a little white residue in one corner; mara said the batteries were not with the radio when she found it.

tom took pictures on his phone, including one of the underside, and then we used the multimeter to check a few points without connecting the receiver to the wall. i did not know what every reading meant. luis explained that he was checking for a direct short across the input, not proving that the set was safe. the numbers changed when he moved one probe, and he said the meter might be picking up the capacitors charging from its own test current. he repeated the check with the leads reversed. tom wrote the readings on a scrap of graph paper, with “not a diagnosis” at the top. this was the first time i had watched someone make a note like that instead of guessing from one measurement.

mara asked about the dial pointer, and tom showed how the cord ran around a little wheel near the tuning capacitor. he thought the pointer might have slipped, but he did not move it because it could be aligned to a mark we could not see from that angle. luis held a flashlight while i looked through the opening. i could see dust and two strings crossing near the pulley, but i could not tell which one was supposed to be tight. tom said, “we should find a service sheet before we start adjusting things.” he thought the receiver might be a common model, but he had not found a model number yet. we looked under the chassis and found a stamped code that looked like “K-214” or maybe “K-2I4,” with the middle mark hard to distinguish.

after that, the talk moved to the club itself. there were two long benches, a rack of hand tools, and a shelf of test gear with paper tags showing who had last borrowed each item. a small oscilloscope had a note saying its probe was missing. tom said the club had received the scope from a school, but he did not know which year. near the sink, someone had taped a card with the next open evening written as the third Thursday. mara said she usually came once or twice a month, depending on work. she asked me if i had ever built a crystal radio. i said i had tried once from a kit as a child, but i remembered more about the tangled wire than the sound.

before we packed up, mara put the cord back in its bag and wrapped the receiver in a cloth she had brought. she said she would look through her uncle’s papers for a manual or another photograph, and tom said he would search the code after the meeting. neither of them said they had identified the fault. i helped return the screwdriver and the meter leads to their labeled drawers. i left at about 9:20, when the rain had stopped but the pavement was still shining. on the bus home, i wrote down the code and the words “cord not safe to use” in my notebook, along with the date. the receiver stayed at the club, on the green mat, with the three trays of screws beside it.", "output": "I went to the Northside Electronics Club on Tuesday evening, mostly because Mara said they were looking at an old shortwave receiver that had belonged to her uncle. I had never been to the club before. It meets in the back room of a community workshop on Ash Street, with the entrance through a side door beside the bicycle racks. I arrived a little after six, while rain was still running off the awning. The room smelled of wet coats, warm dust, and coffee someone had left on a hot plate. Six people were there when I came in, or maybe seven if the person in the doorway was already part of the group.

Mara was setting the receiver on a green cutting mat. “It was working when he put it away, but that could have been ten years ago,” she told me. The case was brown, and its carrying handle had a crack near one screw. A paper label inside the lid read “R. Vale, 1978,” though nobody knew whether that referred to the owner or the year. Mara said it had been kept in a cupboard in her uncle’s shed, but she wasn’t sure if it had ever got damp. She had brought the power cord separately, wrapped in a grocery bag, because its insulation looked stiff. No one plugged it in right away.

Tom, who seemed to run the bench that evening, asked everyone to say what they had brought and hoped to do. He had a small transistor radio with a loose tuning knob and said he was only borrowing the club’s soldering iron. Luis had brought a cardboard box of resistors sorted into envelopes, though some of the handwriting was fading. I had brought a cheap digital multimeter and a notebook, but no project. Mara laughed. “Then you can be the person who remembers which screw came from where.” She had set out three shallow trays beside the receiver, and Tom put the back-panel screws in the first one.

We began by examining the exterior and controls, without applying power. The dial moved smoothly, but the pointer stopped just short of the lower end of the scale. One corner of the front grille was pushed inward, and the case rattled faintly when Tom tilted it. He removed the back panel with a short screwdriver and set it on a folded towel. The wiring looked tidy to me, but a gray film covered the metal shield, and dust had collected around the speaker. Luis pointed to a small stain near the transformer. He said it might just be old adhesive, though he didn’t sound certain. Tom asked us not to brush anything away yet; he wanted a picture before cleaning.

1. Things we checked before applying power
- The power-cord jacket had a split near the plug, so Mara kept it in the bag.
- The fuse holder was present, but the label beside it was too worn to read clearly.
- The speaker cone had no obvious tear, though the paper edge looked dry.
- There was a little white residue in one corner of the battery compartment. Mara said the batteries weren’t with the radio when she found it.

Tom took pictures on his phone, including one of the underside. Then we used the multimeter to check a few points without connecting the receiver to the wall. I didn’t understand what every reading meant. Luis explained that he was checking for a direct short across the input, not proving the set was safe. The numbers changed when he moved one probe. He said the meter might be picking up the capacitors charging from its own test current, and repeated the check with the leads reversed. Tom wrote the readings on a scrap of graph paper, with “not a diagnosis” at the top. It was the first time I’d watched someone make a note like that instead of guessing from a single measurement.

Mara asked about the dial pointer, and Tom showed us how the cord ran around a small wheel near the tuning capacitor. He thought the pointer might have slipped, but didn’t move it because it could be aligned with a mark we couldn’t see from that angle. Luis held a flashlight while I looked through the opening. I could see dust and two strings crossing near the pulley, but couldn’t tell which one was supposed to be tight. “We should find a service sheet before we start adjusting things,” Tom said. He thought the receiver might be a common model, but hadn’t found a model number yet. Under the chassis, we found a stamped code that looked like “K-214” or perhaps “K-2I4”; the middle mark was hard to distinguish.

After that, we talked about the club itself. There were two long benches, a rack of hand tools, and a shelf of test equipment with paper tags showing who had last borrowed each item. A small oscilloscope had a note saying its probe was missing. Tom said the club had received the scope from a school, though he didn’t know which year. Near the sink, someone had taped up a card listing the next open evening as the third Thursday. Mara said she usually came once or twice a month, depending on work. She asked if I had ever built a crystal radio. I said I’d tried once from a kit as a child, but remembered more about the tangled wire than the sound.

Before we packed up, Mara put the cord back in its bag and wrapped the receiver in a cloth she had brought. She said she would look through her uncle’s papers for a manual or another photograph, and Tom said he would search for the code after the meeting. Neither said they had identified the fault. I helped return the screwdriver and meter leads to their labeled drawers. I left at about 9:20, after the rain had stopped but while the pavement was still shining. On the bus home, I wrote down the code and the words “cord not safe to use” in my notebook, along with the date. The receiver stayed at the club on the green mat, with the three trays of screws beside it."}]
